geology_comments: The preferential pyritization of the bacterial fossils (as compared with the algal fossils) suggests that the bacteria inhabited anoxic, iron sulfide-rich muds at the bottom of the basin. If the basin floor could support a bacterial population (which presumably was heterotrophic) but not an algal population (which almost certainly was photoautotrophic), then it is reasonable to infer that the depth of the basin exceeded that of the photic zone. This inference drawn from\r\npaleontological data is consistent with earlier depth estimates of 300 to 800 m (Brown & Plumb in Plumb & Derrick, 1975) drawn from geological data.

lithdescript: Stromatolitic chert. The stromatolites consist largely of a fine mosaic of equant quartz crystals. he fossil site at Bacon Cove is situated in a small cove (Lower Cove) on the southwestern side of Conception Bay (47°29'05.3′′N 53°09'58.1′′W), southeastern Newfoundland, Canada, on lands belonging to the Canadian Crown (Figs. 5 and 6). The outcrop spans c. 200 m of the NNW–SSE-aligned coast.
lithdescript: Thin conglomerate and limestone layers intercalated with coarse red sandstone, siltstone and mudstone with in situ stromatolites12 and microbialites characterise the lowermost c. 2.2 m of the Bonavista Formation at Bacon Cove. Upsection, a c. 4.2-m-thick red limestone is erosively interlayered by a c. 10-mm-thick coarse sandstone bed at c. 3.3 m
geology_comments: The Bonavista Formation is interpreted as a shallow-marine onlap deposit resulting from a NW–SE transgression.

Near junction of Brushy Creek and Saline River in Goosepond Mt. 7.5' quadrangle, Ouachita Mountains
lithdescript: The dark-gray to black limestone clasts [containing fossils] have micritic, microspar, and finely crystalline textures. They are abundant in the channel-form deposits and are supported by a calcareous, bluish-gray shale/slate matrix.
geology_comments: Channel-form debris flows. Clast deposits that occur in channel-form geometries are known from locality A and perhaps also at localities C and F. The best exposed channel (locality A) is approximately 20-25 m across and about 4 m thick. The clasts are lenticular with tapered margins, perhaps in part due to structural stretching, and range in size from less than 1 to about 5 cm thick and from 2 to 30 cm long. Graded bedding is not observed; however, the long axes of the clasts are usually subparallel to bedding...At locality A the upper contact of the debris flow is undulatory and is capped by a carbonate turbidity-flow deposit. The channel-form debris flow deposits at locality A (perhaps also C and F) may represent either proximal flow or flow retained in a channel system.

geogcomments: along Brushy Creek in Goosepond Mt. 7.5' Quad.
lithdescript: dark-gray to black limestone clasts [containing fossils] have micritic, microspar, and finely crystalline textures.
geology_comments:
Sheet-form debris flows. -These deposits have a very high ratio of shale matrix to limestone clasts. Actual geometries of the deposits are difficult to assess because the allochthonous mud matrix is very similar to the surrounding autochthonous
hemipelagic mud. Although the clasts are randomly distributed, their long axes are crudely parallel to the apparent bedding in discrete layers that are tens of centimeters thick, suggesting a sheet-form geometry. Deposits of this type are found at localities B, D, and E and possibly at localities F, K, L, N, and P (see
Figure 1). Distribution of clasts at locality J suggests a multiple sheet-form flow or thicker debris-flow deposit. Competence of the mud matrix presumably was high enough to completely support clasts as large as the scarce small boulders observed at localities L and J. Common clast textures include micritic, microspar,
and finely crystalline limestones and some shales. Clastsize is variable from pebbles to small boulders. Evidence of lithification prior to erosion and redeposition as clasts is indicated by angular fracturing and truncation across internal laminations. Deposits of this type probably represent either unconsolidated
debris over-flow or a more distal facies.

geogcomments: along Brushy Creek in Jessieville 7.5' Quad.
lithdescript: dark-gray to black limestone clasts [containing fossils] have micritic, microspar, and finely crystalline textures.
geology_comments: Sheet-form debris flows. -These deposits have a very high ratio of shale matrix to limestone clasts. Actual geometries of the deposits are difficult to assess because the allochthonous mud matrix is very similar to the surrounding autochthonous hemipelagic mud. Although the clasts are randomly distributed, their long axes are crudely parallel to the apparent bedding in discrete layers that are tens of centimeters thick, suggesting a sheet-form geometry. Deposits of this type are found at localities B, D, and E and possibly at localities F, K, L, N, and P (see Figure 1). Distribution of clasts at locality J suggests a multiple sheet-form flow or thicker debris-flow deposit. Competence of the mud matrix presumably was high enough to completely support clasts as large as the scarce small boulders observed at localities L and J. Common clast textures include micritic, microspar, and finely crystalline limestones and some shales. Clastsize is variable from pebbles to small boulders. Evidence of lithification prior to erosion and redeposition as clasts is indicated by angular fracturing and truncation across internal laminations. Deposits of this type probably represent either unconsolidated debris over-flow or a more distal facies.

geogcomments: along Brushy Creek in Jessieville 7.5' Quad.
lithdescript: dark-gray to black limestone clasts [containing fossils] have micritic, microspar, and finely crystalline textures.
geology_comments:
Sheet-form debris flows. -These deposits have a very high ratio of shale matrix to limestone clasts. Actual geometries of the deposits are difficult to assess because the allochthonous mud matrix is very similar to the surrounding autochthonous
hemipelagic mud. Although the clasts are randomly distributed, their long axes are crudely parallel to the apparent bedding in discrete layers that are tens of centimeters thick, suggesting a sheet-form geometry. Deposits of this type are found at localities B, D, and E and possibly at localities F, K, L, N, and P (see
Figure 1). Distribution of clasts at locality J suggests a multiple sheet-form flow or thicker debris-flow deposit. Competence of the mud matrix presumably was high enough to completely support clasts as large as the scarce small boulders observed at localities L and J. Common clast textures include micritic, microspar,
and finely crystalline limestones and some shales. Clastsize is variable from pebbles to small boulders. Evidence of lithification prior to erosion and redeposition as clasts is indicated by angular fracturing and truncation across internal laminations. Deposits of this type probably represent either unconsolidated
debris over-flow or a more distal facies.

geogcomments: INFORMATION  The sheet-like fossils described in this paper are from an exposure about 300 m northeast of Horse Thief Springs, Kingston Range, southeastern California. To locate this exposure, start at Horse Thief Springs and drive about 0.3 km east to the first prominent gully on the north side of the road (there is sufficient room to park there). Walk north up the gully 157 m from the north edge of the road (or 42 m north of the north end of the prominent dolomite outcrop that forms a prominent "wall" on the west side of the gully).\r\n\r\nUniversal Transverse Mercator Coordinates (Zone 11) of the type locality are approx 3959320 m north and 600785 m east, U. S. Geological Survey Horse Thief Springs, California ( 1984 provisional edition) 7.5' Topographic Quadrangle.
lithdescript: One meter east of the gully bottom is the following sequence, which is presented in stratigraphic order: 0.7 m of well exposed, massive dolomite: 3.4 m of intermittently exposed dolomite and mudstone along with covered intervals; 1.6 m of well exposed dolomite with chert in the lower one-half of the unit; and 0.8 m covered followed by more than 10 m of siltstone and mudstone. The fossils described in this paper are from the lower cherty interval in the 1.6 m thick dolomite unit. They also occur in chert and dolomite at this locality about 15 m higher in the section.

lithdescript: clays, mudstones. The upper part of the formation (the interval of 480–478.7 m) is composed of thinly interbedded greenish gray hydromica-kaolinite mudstones and micaceous siltstones
clays, mudstones. The upper part of the formation (the interval of 480–478.7 m) is composed of thinly interbedded greenish gray hydromica-kaolinite mudstones and micaceous siltstones

The formation is represented by greenish gray, gray, variegated in the upper part of the section, micaceous, glauconite-bearing siltstones with lenses and thin interlayers of mudstones, clays of kaolinite-hydromica composition and feldspar-quartz sandstones with clay-dolomite cement of pore type, or, less frequently, with poikilitic gypsum cement. geology_comments: All priapulid fossils are found in yellowish to greenish mudstone of the Wulongqing Formation. The mudstone layers normally show sharp and erosive bases and are fining upwards, ranging from 0.5 cm to 2 cm in thickness. Multiple graded silt-mud couplets are commonly observed. Complete and articulated palaeoscolecidans are mostly preserved in the layers with low-grade or no bioturbation. The living environment of the Guanshan Biota was reconstructed as a storm-dominated offshore transition, between fair-weather wave base and storm wave base, and within the photic zone, 40–50 m in depth

lithdescript: That is, in part, because much of the McKay Group in this region consists of a monotonous and uniform sequence of calcareous shale, with few interbedded thin calcareous units that can be used as markers to subdivide it.
geology_comments: The calcareous shale and marl of the McKay Group in the Bull River Valley are typical of the Outer Detrital Belt, a lithofacies characterizing distal shelf environments of Laurentia during most of the Cambrian (Palmer, 1973; Aitken, 1978, 1997; Peters and Gaines, 2012). They are often finely laminated and contain only rare, thin tempestites, suggesting that most of these beds were deposited below the storm weather wave base. An open-marine, deep-water environment is also suggested by the trilobite assemblages, which best compare to comparatively deep-water Furongian faunas of Nevada (Emigrant Formation), South China, and Korea (Chatterton and Gibb, 2016). These trilobite assemblages are characterized by unusually high proportions of articulated specimens (Chatterton et al., 1994; Chatterton and Ludvigsen, 1998; Chatterton and Gibb, 2016), which speaks to a low energy depositional environment, possibly periodically depleted in oxygen. The presence of barren intervals, the total absence of burrows, and the fact that olenids (e.g.Wujiajiania) are particularly abundant in somebeds, but rare to absent in lithologically similar horizons, are also suggestive of frequent episodes of oxygen depletion on the sea floor (Chatterton and Gibb, 2016).

lithdescript: consists primarily of medium gray, thin- to thick bedded limestone with dark shale interbeds and intervals rich in laminated chert.
geology_comments: Deposition of the basal member under shallow subtidal conditions was followed by significant deepening that initiated accumulation of the chert-rich, deep marine facies that characterize the Catlin Member. We interpret the prominent fine laminations of the lime mudstone rhythmically interbedded with dark shale (Figure 2.2, 2.7), and retained by the chert identified in early studies as a defining attribute of the Catlin Member, as an indication that these beds originated as dilute carbonate turbidites. The scattered bioclastic grainstone beds and lenses in the Catlin were formed by localized winnowing during occasional, higher energy events that concentrated skeletal fragments into coquinoid lags. (Taylor et al. 2024)

geogcomments: "east of Ait Youb in the Lemdad Syncline, High Atlas Mountains, Morocco"
lithdescript: pyroclastic layer; "sheet-like unit dominated by thick-bedded sandstones (fig. S1). Volcanic activity was prevalent at the time of deposition" "The sandstone beds consist of medium-to fine-grained hummocky cross-stratified feldspar-rich to lithic sandstone, and medium- to coarse-grained trough cross-bedded lithic sandstone with pebbly layers dominated by volcanic clasts. Layers of cream- to white-coloured, fine-grained volcanic ash are recognized by mineral content and texture (fig. S2). A few thin interbeds of green to grey mudstone are also preserved within these amalgamated sandstones."
geology_comments: "shallow marine, storm- and wave-dominated shoreface to foreshore setting"

lithdescript:
A petrographic analysis of the El Gavil´ an Formation revealed 
mudstone, floatstone, wackestone, and packstone. These rocks contain 
fragments of chancelloriids, brachiopods, and trilobites. Additionally, 
shale and calcareous siltstone are also found in this formation. Based on 
the petrographic analysis, it can be inferred that these rocks were 
deposited in a low-energy environment.

The dominant lithology of this unit is calcareous siltstone with in
tercalations of mudstone. In thin section, no bioclasts were observed, 
only pellets. In addition, the abundance of porifers in the unit could 
indicate a low-energy environment. Trilobites from the Agnostida, 
Ptychopariida, Corynexochida, and Asaphida are observed in this unit, 
consistent with the marine environment of the open outer platform in 
central Sonora and the Great Basin of the western United States of 
America.

tercalations of mudstone. In thin section, no bioclasts were observed, 
only pellets. In addition, the abundance of porifers in the unit could 
indicate a low-energy environment. Trilobites from the Agnostida, 
Ptychopariida, Corynexochida, and Asaphida are observed in this unit, 
consistent with the marine environment of the open outer platform in 
central Sonora and the Great Basin of the western United States of 
America.

Thin sections reveal grainstone with an abundant fauna of trilobites 
and brachiopods, bioclastic packstone, wackestone with partial dolo
mite replacement, and very fine-grained sandstone with clays and bio
clasts. The trilobite fauna is represented mainly by ptychopariids and 
together with the lithology characterize an inner platform marine 
environment fluctuating toward a restricted inner platform marine 
environment due to the influence of terrigenous input into carbonate 
rocks. This is analogous to the biofacies model of the Great Basin in the 
western United States of America.

with undulating and parallel stratification. Petrographic analysis in
dicates a low-energy environment developed on an outer marine 
platform.

The Mistaken Point Formation is dominated by fine to medium-grained turbidites interspersed with thin interturbidite siltstone beds that contain the fossil horizons (Narbonne et al., 2001; Wood et al., 2003). These fossil beds are covered by a veneer of volcanic ash, which smothered the frondose organisms and accelerated the lithification process, thereby allowing for the preservation of high-relief fossil fronds on upper bedding plane surfaces. The crystal size of the tuff preserving the fossils limits the fidelity of the finer structure discernible in Mistaken Point fronds.
geology_comments: See WOOD, D. A., R. W. DALRYMPLE, G. M. NARBONNE, J. G. GEHLING, AND M. E. CLAPHAM. 2003. Paleoenvironmental analysis of the late Neoproterozoic Mistaken Point and Trepassey formations, southeastern Newfoundland. Canadian Journal of Earth Sciences, 40:1375–1391.

This assemblage comprises greenish-gray, fine-grained, thin-bedded, crossbedded, and planar-laminated sandstones. The sandstones are channel fills that appear in lenses and laterally discontinuous packages (0.3–1.8 m thick and up to 10 m wide) with convex downward bases and nearly flat upper surfaces. These lenses occur on surfaces that are characterized by numerous sand-filled scour casts. Cross-bedded sandstone units tend to consist of multistoried cross-laminations. Individual sandstone beds (0.1–0.4 m) are another element of stratification. They record strong current influence and exhibit a variety of sole marks, including load casts, chevron, drag, and flute marks, current crescents, and gutter casts. \r\n\r\nThis assemblage comprises packages (1.0–1.5 m) of gray and yellowishgray, fine-grained, thin-bedded sandstone units (0.1–0.5 m) interbedded with intervals (0.3–0.5 m up to 2 m thick) of graded siltstoneshale couplets and abundant gutter casts. The sandstone beds have sharp bases, fine upwards, and have rippled tops. Thinner beds tend to consist of fine horizontal laminations. Some of them contain gently curved laminasets which probably represent hummocky stratification. However, thicker units exhibit fining-upward textures, convoluted laminations, amalgamation surfaces, ball-and-pillow structure, isolated shale clasts, and wave ripple laminations.

geogcomments: A fragmented slab was collected from outcrop in the area of Aar Farm, east of Aus, southwestern Namibia. The sandstone unit is part of the Kliphoek Member of the Dabis Formation, Kuibis Subgroup, Nama Group (terminal Proterozoic-Cambrian)
lithdescript: planar laminated sheet sandstone with graded bedding, and samples three event beds, each having variable (40±50 mm)thickness. Their lower bedding planes are erosional and preserve flat clay pebbles, which are chip-shaped rather than compressed mud balls, recognized by the occurrence of inclined axes. These chips consist of maroon and grey mudstone and may reach 18mm in diameter. Rather than being contained to a sharp bedding plane, they float within the lowermost sandy matrix and are interpreted as a lag deposit of a turbidite-like flow. Kliphoek Member sandstone in general records strong current influence and may be fluvial in origin (Germs 1983; Saylor et al. 1995). Each bed contains a succession of two distinct assemblages of Pteridinium, interpreted as winnowed and virgin (undisturbed).

lithdescript: [T]he Shibantan Member is composed of dark grey, thin-bedded bituminous limestone with intercalated chert layers and concretions.
geology_comments: It is previously interpreted to have been deposited on a carbonate intra-ramp lagoon (Q Xiao et al., 2020), and more specifically in a subtidal environment below fair-weather wave base (Xiao et al., 2005; Shen et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014; Meyer et al., 2014; Duda et al., 2016). Bedding surfaces of the Shibantan Member have wrinkled surfaces and crinkled micro-laminae interpreted as representing evidence for microbial mats (Chen et al., 2013), which may have played a key role in the preservation of soft-bodied Ediacaran organisms (Gehling, 1999; Callow and Brasier, 2009; Slagter et al., 2022). Microbial mats, along with abundant macroalgal fossils such as Flabellophyton (Wan et al., 2020) and Vendotaenia (Zhao et al., 1988), indicate deposition within the photic zone.

geogcomments: Parker Quarry, Franklin County, Vermont
lithdescript: The mudstone-dominated strata of the Parker Formation at Parker's Cobble have undergone low-grade metamorphism resulting in a bedding-parallel cleavage, which facilitates splitting. Sedimentary features are largely obscured in the field by pyrite weathering, which stains surfaces with iron oxides, but they are clearly revealed in polished slabs. The soft-bodied fossils occur in claystone event beds that, combined with evidence for graded bedding and a lack of wave influence, indicate deposition from mud-rich flows below storm wave base.

geogcomments: Quanjishan area, northern Qaidam Basin, Tibetan Plateau, Northwest China, Quanjishan section A (37°25′55.2″N, 95°48′0.2″E), Qaidam Basin
lithdescript: Fossils were collected in bottom half of unit, in siltstones and interbedded sandstones.\r\n"The Zhoujieshan Formation is about 57 m in thickness in the Quanjishan area, and consists of a ca. 7 m thick cap dolostone unit at the base, followed by ca. 50 m of siliciclastic rocks (Fig. 3A, B, C, G). The cap dolostone unit comprises basal massive, pebble-bearing dolostones, which gradually transition to pebble-free, thick–medium bedded dolostones (Fig. 2; Shen et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2022). The siliciclastic and dolomitic clasts in the lower part of the cap dolostone unit are interpreted to be either debris falling from ice rafts during the deglacial period, or products of transgressive reworking of the underlying unlithified diamictites of the Hongtiegou Formation, indicating a continuous transition between these two unit"
geology_comments: "the Zhoujieshan Formation was deposited somewhere between the lower shoreface and offshore transition, where hydrodynamic conditions are typically moderate to low, with occasional influxes of higher energy sediment from storm events."

geology_comments: Regionally, facies of the Mount Clark and Mount Cap formations record the evolution from a nearshore to deeper water environment (MacNaughton et al., 2013; Herbers et al., 2016; Handkamer, 2020; Sommers et al., 2020). In the present study area, low-angle cross-bedded, wavy bedded, and wave-rippled sandstone with minor glauconite of the Mount Clark Formation indicate a nearshore setting (Handkamer, 2020). The dominance of storm-induced features, with rare sand bars, suggest a relatively low-energy stormdominated shoreline with weak tidal influence. In distal sections of the Mount Clark Formation, interbedded sandstone and siltstone with wave ripples, gutter casts, local hummocky crossstratification, and minor unidirectional ripples (Handkamer, 2020) record fluctuating conditions produced by storms in the offshore setting. Interbedded, rippled sandy grainstone and argillaceous lime mudstone (Handkamer, 2020) represent similar conditions during episodes of localized carbonate production. Strata of the Mount Clark Formation are dominated by a deposit-feeding ichnofauna (Handkamer, 2020). The scarcity of burrows cast by tempestites in the offshore setting is attributed to scour during deposition. A vertical, suspension-feeding ichnofauna is dominant in strata representing upper-shoreface deposits (Handkamer, 2020), due to organic productivity in the water column.

lithdescript: Limestone: sandy trilobite biomicrite; scattered fine pelsparite. Fine quartz sand content decreases upsection to zero above 1,235 feet. Scattered intraclasts in lower 40 feet of unit; scattered oosparite beds from 1,216 to 1,225 feet. Scattered scarce glauconite and ferro an dolomite. Medium grayish brown, mostly thin to medium slabby beds with some thick beds in upper 80 feet of unit. Weathers light to medium gray to grayish brown.

Limestone: trilobite biomicrite; intraclastic biosparite bed at 820 feet. Scarce very fine quartz sand, ferroan dolomite, and linguloid brachiopods; scattered pelsparite. Medium grayish brown, mostly medium to thick beds; weathers light to medium gray. Brown dolomite stringers on some weathered surfaces.

Limestone: mostly trilobite biomicrite and pelsparite; scattered biosparite. Very fine quartz sand common but decreasing toward top of unit; intraclasts scarce. Medium to light grayish brown, mostly medium to thick beds that weather light to medium gray. Thin-bedded, predominantly brown-weathering pelsparite from 720 to 750 feet. Silicified Billingsella at 695, 720, 730, 733, and 751 feet. Brown dolomitic stringers common on weathered surfaces.

geogcomments: The Xiaoshiba Biota herein is located in the eastern suburb of Kunming in southern China (Fig. 1A–B; Yang et al., 2013, 2014, 2015; Hou et al., 2017) where the Cambrian (Series 2) Hongjingshao Formation is widely exposed (Luo et al., 1994, 2008).
lithdescript: Hongjingshao Formation is widely exposed (Luo et al., 1994, 2008). The Hongjingshao Formation in the Kunming area is up to 180 m thick and mainly consists of medium to thick bedded sandstones and thin bedded siltstones (Luo et al., 2008, p. 28), containing two successive biotas: the Xiaoshiba (Yang et al., 2013) and the Malong (Luo et al., 2008). The Xiaoshiba Biota is located in the most basal part of the Hongjingshao Formation and is characteristic of a thick-bedded sandstone unit occa- sionally interspersed with thin-bedded siltstones, shales or mudstones. Stratigraphically it is evidently higher than the Chengjiang Biota but obviously lower than the Malong Biota.\nThe approximately 0.9-m-thick mudstone which has yielded those specimens of Z. typica (Hou et al., 2017) also hosts the macroalgae described in this paper (Fig. 1C). These macroalgae are located in the lower part of the approximate 0.9-m-thick mudstone, where Z. typica and other animals are scarcely preserved. The mechanism behind the preservation of the macroalgae and metazoans is unknown, but the different spacial division of them may reflect diverse taphonomic requirements.

geogcomments: The fossils originate from the Terreneuvian Kessyusa Group of the Olenek Uplift (northeastern Siberian Platform) (Fig. 1)... The collection... from the section 0705 (left bank of the Khorbusuonka River; 71°17′30′′N, 123°46′30′′E; Fig. 1.3).
lithdescript: The sections in the northeast, including the one where the studied fossils were found (section 0705; left bank of the Khorbusuonka River; 71°17′30′′N, 123°46′30′′E; Fig. 1.3), are composed mainly of cross-bedded and hummocky cross-stratified calcareous sandstones and ooidal and sandy limestones (Grazhdankin et al., 2020). The studied fossils are localized in parallel-laminated and hummocky cross-stratified sandy limestones (grainstones). The grainstones are composed of rounded to poorly rounded fine sand and silt grains (60–100 μm) of calcite, quartz, ilmenite, and rutile with sporadic ooids (Ivanovskaya et al., 2019; Fig. 1.1). The grains are cemented with fine sparitic calcite. The previously proposed correlation suggests this level corresponds to the base and lower part of the Suordakh Member in the central Olenek Uplift.

lithdescript:
Fossils on the Matthews Surface are preserved as
negative impressions on the upper bedding surface of a
fine siltstone, immediately overlain by a thin layer of
tuff/tuffite (Fig. 3A) that is inferred to have smothered
the community in situ as an obrution deposit (cf.
Seilacher, 1999). The negative impressions left on the siltstone by the decomposed organisms were cast by collapse of the overlying tuff onto the surface. In the case of stems preserved in positive relief the tuff is considered to have lithified before decomposition of the stem tissues, resulting in the upper surface being cast (Fig. 3A, B, cf. Gehling, 1999). Counterparts to the impressions can sometimes be found on the bottom of the overlying tuffaceous layer (Fig. 3A, B).
geology_comments: The lithologies of these Charnia-bearing Ediacaran-aged rocks reveal sedimentary environments ranging from deep basinal to mid-slope settings, particularly in association with sandstones, siltstones and tuffites, which are strongly influenced by density currents (Ichaso et al., 2007; Matthews et al., 2020; McIlroy et al., 2022; Wood et al., 2003).

lithdescript: The upper carbonate member is 22.2m thick. At its base is an interval of sandy bioclastic grainstone 1.7 m thick, followed by 11.5 m of dolomite-mottled, dominantly bioturbated wackestone with locally interbedded grainstone and several small archaeocyath-bearing bioherms up to 30 cm in diameter and 20 cm thick. This is overlain by 7 m of mostly thin-bedded grainstone with meter-sized bioherms containing archaeocyaths and modular coral-like skeletons and capped by 2 m of dolomitized grainstone with intercalated siltstone laminae.

The upper carbonate member is almost 72 m thick (Fritz and Mountjoy, 1975). It appears to be mostly dolomitized thin-bedded grainstone with scattered bioherms. At the top is a limestone interval ~4 m thick with an undulating upper surface conforming to variably coalesced bioherms separated by grainstone-filled inter-mound areas less than 1m across.

identified_name: Hallidaya brueri n. gen. n. sp.
geogcomments: The main fossil occurrence lies almost on a direct line between Kennecott Explorations’ drill-holes Mt. Skinner No. 2 and No. 3 (text-fig. 2), on the sides of a small valley running ENE.-WSW. On the south side of the valley, the fossils have been found through about 20 ft. of maroon sandstones and minor shales above a green band which measured 16 ft. thick (where it was intercepted by the drillhole Mt. Skinner No. 2) and in the green band. On the north side they were encountered more sparsely below and in the green band which here forms a dip slope and is strongly weathered, outcropping poorly. Except on the steeper slopes of the valley, scree and rainwash material covers much of the outcrop. One piece of float containing a fossil was found in the creek between Mt. Skinner No. 2 and the main fossil outcrop; it is most probably from a further occurrence of the fossils along the strike of the beds.
lithdescript: maroon sandstones and minor shales.\r\n\r\nA petrological report on samples of maroon and greenish, coarse and fine sediments was supplied to Kennecott Explorations by Australian Mineral Development Laboratories (Appendix to Kennecott final report, Mt. Skinner Examination, Northern Territory). It indicated that the sediments generally may be classified as subgreywackes and impure siltstones to claystones. The coarser sediments are more strongly cemented by authigenic quartz, and the red coloration is induced by iron oxides coating the detrital grains, whether of quartz, rock-fragments, or feldspar. The green bands contain copper minerals and lack iron oxide coatings on detrital grains. Where there is clay cement present (as, particularly, in the finer beds) there is less authigenic quartz. Laths of authigenic mica are present, and there is more evidence of stress and metamorphic change reported from the petrological study than would be expected from field evidence. The lithological setting has numerous parallels with the Precambrian fossiliferous deposits at Ediacara (Wade 1968), though these lack rock fragments and have much less detrital mica (Goldring and Curnow 1967).

geogcomments: Sample RS/f411, Locality 1, between Mt. Jamroga and Helix Pass. "upper\npart of a discontinuously exposed section, about 850 m thick, through the Spurs Formation in a col along the ridge separating the catchments of the Carryer and Sledgers Glaciers in the Bowers Mountains, 4 km to the southwest of Helix Pass"
lithdescript: "The section (Fig. 2) essentially comprises dark calcareous shales and siltstones with dark silty\nlimestone interbeds and lenses up to 15 cm thick. Both the siltstone and silty limestones are pyritic\nin places."
geology_comments: "The lithology and sedimentary structures suggest an offshore, outer shelf to upper slope, depositional environment"

geogcomments: The Moro section is located approximately 5 km south of Moro Gorge on the north-eastern limb of the Arrowie Syncline, a ~ 25 km long south-west plunging syncline located immediately north of the Stirrup Iron Range.
geology_comments: 59 m of an archaeocyath-Renalcis biohermal facies. These build-ups formed large mound-like structures that measure up to 100 m in lateral extent (an example is transected by the Moro section) and occur for more than 2 km along strike to the north of the section line. Biohermal architecture in the Hideaway Well Member consists of a build-up of closely spaced regular and irregular archaeocyaths bound together by envelopes of encrusting calcimicrobes such as Girvanella, Renalcis and Epiphyton, in addition to irregular archaeocyaths that facilitated sequential biohermal accretion and topographic relief above the surrounding shelf sediments. The flanks of the bioherms are dissected by deep, narrow channels filled with intraclastic carbonate, fragmented shelly debris and micrite that were shed into deeper lagoonal or outer shelf-slope environments. Localised archaeocyath bioherms such as the one transected by the Moro section line are a common feature on the extensive shallow water platform represented by the Wilkawillina Limestone in the Wirrealpa Hinge Zone sensu Gravestock and Cowley (1995).

geology_comments: The "bimodal" mixture of sand and shale may indicate proximity to shoreline, in which case this may be too shallow for inclusion, but presence of silt and confinement of clastics to distinct layers argues against this; "deeper water environment affected by ... fluxoturbidites"

identified_name: Turbanicystis inflatus n. gen. n. sp.
geogcomments: The material described in this paper comes from the Miaobanpo (fossil) Quarry which is excavated near the top of an east-west trending mountain ridge about two kilometers north of the village of Balang, Jianhe County, Guizhou Province.
lithdescript: These deeper water sediments are primarily black to greenish black, shale to silt-sized siliciclastics. Bedding in the form of fine laminae is mostly from suspension obrution sedimentation. ... Disruption of sedimentation on any scale is rare with an almost total lack of bioturbation. There is little evidence for unidirectional flow, but some levels show alignment of equal sized specimens resting on current-swept surfaces.
geology_comments: Deposition is interpreted to be between 150 to 200 m water depth along the outer shelf to upper slope of the Jiangnan Slope belt on the eastern margin of the South China (Yangtze) Platform (Lin et al., 2008).

geogcomments: "southern Salt Spring Hills in California (35°36’39.96"N, 116°16’3.36"W)"
lithdescript: "The upper member consists of mixed siltstones and fossiliferous grainstones, which have been regionally dolomitized (Stewart, 1970; Diehl, 1979) (Fig. 3.1). The upper member contains abundant early Cambrian fossils, including trilobites, brachiopods, echinoderms, hyoliths, Volborthella, Salterella, archaeocyaths, and complex trace fossils (Stewart, 1970; Nelson, 1978; Langille, 1979; Licari and Licari, 1987, 1999; Hagadorn and Waggoner, 2002; Mata et al., 2012), and it is interpreted to have been deposited in a shallow-marine setting influenced by tides and storms (Stewart, 1970; Diehl, 1979)."

geogcomments: Nine Mile Canyon - Antelope Range
lithdescript: consists primarily of medium gray, thin- to thick bedded limestone with dark shale interbeds and intervals rich in laminated chert.
geology_comments: Deposition of the basal member under shallow subtidal conditions was followed by significant deepening that initiated accumulation of the chert-rich, deep marine facies that characterize the Catlin Member. We interpret the prominent fine laminations of the lime mudstone rhythmically interbedded with dark shale (Figure 2.2, 2.7), and retained by the chert identified in early studies as a defining attribute of the Catlin Member, as an indication that these beds originated as dilute carbonate turbidites. The scattered bioclastic grainstone beds and lenses in the Catlin were formed by localized winnowing during occasional, higher energy events that concentrated skeletal fragments into coquinoid lags. (Taylor et al. 2024)

lithdescript: This assemblage comprises greenish-gray, fine-grained, thin-bedded, crossbedded, and planar-laminated sandstones. The sandstones are channel fills that appear in lenses and laterally discontinuous packages (0.3–1.8 m thick and up to 10 m wide) with convex downward bases and nearly flat upper surfaces. These lenses occur on surfaces that are characterized by numerous sand-filled scour casts. Cross-bedded sandstone units tend to consist of multistoried cross-laminations. Individual sandstone beds (0.1–0.4 m) are another element of stratification. They record strong current influence and exhibit a variety of sole marks, including load casts, chevron, drag, and flute marks, current crescents, and gutter casts. \r\n\r\nThis assemblage comprises packages (1.0–1.5 m) of gray and yellowishgray, fine-grained, thin-bedded sandstone units (0.1–0.5 m) interbedded with intervals (0.3–0.5 m up to 2 m thick) of graded siltstoneshale couplets and abundant gutter casts. The sandstone beds have sharp bases, fine upwards, and have rippled tops. Thinner beds tend to consist of fine horizontal laminations. Some of them contain gently curved laminasets which probably represent hummocky stratification. However, thicker units exhibit fining-upward textures, convoluted laminations, amalgamation surfaces, ball-and-pillow structure, isolated shale clasts, and wave ripple laminations.

geogcomments: A fragmented slab was collected from outcrop in the area of Aar Farm, east of Aus, southwestern Namibia. The sandstone unit is part of the Kliphoek Member of the Dabis Formation, Kuibis Subgroup, Nama Group (terminal Proterozoic-Cambrian)
lithdescript: planar laminated sheet sandstone with graded bedding, and samples three event beds, each having variable (40±50 mm)thickness. Their lower bedding planes are erosional and preserve flat clay pebbles, which are chip-shaped rather than compressed mud balls, recognized by the occurrence of inclined axes. These chips consist of maroon and grey mudstone and may reach 18mm in diameter. Rather than being contained to a sharp bedding plane, they float within the lowermost sandy matrix and are interpreted as a lag deposit of a turbidite-like flow. lithdescript: This assemblage comprises greenish-gray, fine-grained, thin-bedded, crossbedded, and planar-laminated sandstones. The sandstones are channel fills that appear in lenses and laterally discontinuous packages (0.3–1.8 m thick and up to 10 m wide) with convex downward bases and nearly flat upper surfaces. These lenses occur on surfaces that are characterized by numerous sand-filled scour casts. Cross-bedded sandstone units tend to consist of multistoried cross-laminations. Individual sandstone beds (0.1–0.4 m) are another element of stratification. They record strong current influence and exhibit a variety of sole marks, including load casts, chevron, drag, and flute marks, current crescents, and gutter casts. \r\n\r\nThis assemblage comprises packages (1.0–1.5 m) of gray and yellowishgray, fine-grained, thin-bedded sandstone units (0.1–0.5 m) interbedded with intervals (0.3–0.5 m up to 2 m thick) of graded siltstoneshale couplets and abundant gutter casts. The sandstone beds have sharp bases, fine upwards, and have rippled tops. Thinner beds tend to consist of fine horizontal laminations. Some of them contain gently curved laminasets which probably represent hummocky stratification. However, thicker units exhibit fining-upward textures, convoluted laminations, amalgamation surfaces, ball-and-pillow structure, isolated shale clasts, and wave ripple laminations.

Wirrapowie Limestone (sequence ∈1.1) The Wirrapowie and Wilkawillina Limestones are coeval carbonate facies representing adjacent, interﬁngering platform and restricted lagoonal palaeoenvironments, respectively (Haslett, 1975)(Fig. 12). Lack of cross-bedding, quartz grains and other coarse detrital material indicate a predominantly low energy regime, and lack of mud-cracks, halite casts and other evidence of subaerial exposure indicates that the environment remained consistently submerged (Haslett, 1975). lithdescript: [T]he Shibantan Member is composed of dark grey, thin-bedded bituminous limestone with intercalated chert layers and concretions.
geology_comments: It is previously interpreted to have been deposited on a carbonate intra-ramp lagoon (Q Xiao et al., 2020), and more specifically in a subtidal environment below fair-weather wave base (Xiao et al., 2005; Shen et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014; Meyer et al., 2014; Duda et al., 2016). Bedding surfaces of the Shibantan Member have wrinkled surfaces and crinkled micro-laminae interpreted as representing evidence for microbial mats (Chen et al., 2013), which may have played a key role in the preservation of soft-bodied Ediacaran organisms (Gehling, 1999; Callow and Brasier, 2009; Slagter et al., 2022). Microbial mats, along with abundant macroalgal fossils such as Flabellophyton (Wan et al., 2020) and Vendotaenia (Zhao et al., 1988), indicate deposition within the photic zone.

geogcomments: Outcrop is located on the left bank of the Sylvitsa River, a tributary of the Chusovaya River, in the Central Urals (58°0100400N, 58°4001500E).
lithdescript: The stratotype section of the Konovalovka Member is located on the left bank of the Sylvitsa River in the northern part of the Konovalovka Stow (outcrop 0531) (Fig. 1). This section is composed of a complex sequence of siliciclastic sediments. The informal ‘lower’ part of the Konovalovka Member consists of c. 15 m of predominantly thin-bedded siltstones with lenticular sandstone interbeds. These sandstones exhibit wave-rippled and unidirectional cross-bedding, indicative of shallow-water deposition influenced by wave and current activity. The informal ‘upper’ part of the Konovalovka Member is a c. 85-m-thick sequence of finely alternating siltstones and shales with interbeds of wave-rippled sandstones. A distinguishing feature of this interval is the presence of fine, sub-millimetric, wavy,\ncrinkly, dark grey carbonaceous laminae interbedded with siltstone or sandstone, previously interpreted as biolamination (Bobkov et al. 2019; Mitchell et al. 2020) or otherwise known as textured organic surfaces (Gehling & Droser 2009).
geology_comments: These deposits were previously interpreted as reflecting low-energy, lagoonal or prodeltaic conditions (Grazhdankin et al. 2009, 2010; Bobkov et al. 2019).
